content.text: Results are noisy, so I'm repeating tests on two recombination tasks. If the learner is part-based, they should cost the same, because neither has any new rules.

input.command: python3 query.py submit '{"verdict": "holistic", "confidence": 0.75, "justification": "Trained L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2, L3-S3-M3 so every rule labelled 1-3 was familiar, then tested recombinations (0 new rules), tasks with 1-2 new rules, and L4-S4-M4 (3 new rules). Part-based predicts that all recombinations cost the same and that cost rises with the number of new rules. Instead, two recombinations that both have 0 new rules differed reliably: L2-S3-M1 mean 13.1 (n=12, often 1) and L2-S1-M3 mean 27.4 (n=11), t about 2.8. L2-S1-M3 cost about the same as the 3-new-rule task L4-S4-M4 (mean 29, n=11). Tasks with 1 new rule (mean 30) and 2 new rules (mean 25) were not ordered by how many rules were new. Cost depends on which task it is rather than on how many rules are new, which fits a holistic learner with an unseen similarity measure. Output overlap from compare did not fully explain the costs. Tests were very noisy (SD about 12), so confidence is moderate."}'

content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.75. I used 59 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3, so every rule numbered 1–3 was familiar and only the rules numbered 4 were new. I then tested three kinds of task:
- **Recombinations** (no new rules), such as L2-S3-M1 and L2-S1-M3.
- **Tasks with 1 or 2 new rules**, such as L1-S4-M1 and L4-S4-M1.
- **L4-S4-M4**, the only task with all 3 rules new.

**Results** (mean examples to criterion; lower means easier):

| Task | New rules | Mean | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| L2-S3-M1 | 0 | 13.1 | 12 |
| L2-S1-M3 | 0 | 27.4 | 11 |
| Tasks with 1 new rule | 1 | ~30 | 8 |
| Tasks with 2 new rules | 2 | ~25 | 4 |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | ~29 | 11 |

**Reasoning:**
- A part-based learner should find every recombination equally easy, and cost should rise with the number of new rules.
- Instead, the two recombinations differed reliably (a t-statistic of about 2.8), even though neither had any new rules.
- L2-S1-M3 cost about the same as L4-S4-M4, even though one has no new rules and the other has three.
- The number of new rules did not order the costs.

Cost seems to depend on which task it is rather than on how many of its rules are new. That fits a holistic learner using a similarity measure we can't see.

**Caveats:** Individual test results were very noisy (they ranged from 1 to 51), so the main difference rests on about two standard errors. The output overlap reported by `compare` did not fully explain the costs, so I couldn't confirm what similarity measure the learner uses.
